**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

1. A Tavily general search was made for:  
   “Wirecard Jan Marsalek public statements audit findings missing trust account cash regulator failures disappearance verified facts sources”

2. A reasoning/reflection tool was used to identify that the initial search provided:
   - Wirecard’s own 28 April 2020 announcement concerning the KPMG special investigation; and
   - A European Parliament-commissioned policy study concerning failures across the defenses against corporate fraud.  
   The reflection also noted that the available results did not yet cover the full five dimensions, particularly the 2019–2020 audit chronology, trust-account evidence, and verified facts or unknowns concerning Jan Marsalek’s disappearance.

3. Three parallel Tavily general searches were made for:
   - “site:wirecard.com 18 June 2020 trustee accounts 1.9 billion EY statement”
   - “Wirecard KPMG special audit report trust accounts 1.9 billion EY 18 June 2020 primary source”
   - “Jan Marsalek disappearance verified facts 19 June 2020 whereabouts official investigation source”
   - “Jan Marsalek disappeared Munich June 2020 verified facts prosecutor source”
   - “Wirecard parliamentary inquiry report BaFin FREP APAS failures official source”

4. A further Tavily general search was made for:
   - “Wirecard Jan Marsalek disappearance June 2020 official facts source ID”
   - “Wirecard missing 1.9 billion trust accounts audit report source ID”
   - “Wirecard EY audit certificate 2020 no evidence 1.9 billion source”

5. The repeated searches returned the same two benchmark sources, with source IDs **SRC-001** and **SRC-002**. No additional source record was supplied in the tool outputs.

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. Wirecard public statements, disclosures, and representations

### 1.1 Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 disclosure

Wirecard AG issued an announcement dated **28 April 2020 at 07:52 CET/CEST**, described as a disclosure of inside information under Article 17 of the Market Abuse Regulation. The announcement was transmitted by DGAP, and the announcement stated that “the issuer is solely responsible for the content of this announcement.” [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard stated that it had received the special audit report from the auditing company KPMG “in the early hours of today, April 28 2020.” Wirecard stated that the report would be published as soon as possible under its transparency webpage. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard represented that:

> “Incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance sheet forgery has not been identified.” [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard further stated that, with respect to all four areas of the audit—Third Party Acquiring business, Merchant Cash Advance/Digital Lending, and business activities in India and Singapore—“no significant findings have been made, which would require an adjustment of the annual accounts 2016-2018.” [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard stated that, during the audits of the annual accounts for 2016–2018, the available documents and audit measures were sufficient to prove the revenues in the Third Party Acquiring business. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard also stated that, under KPMG’s increased forensic requirements, not all data that would have been required to prove the revenues in those years could be obtained because the required data were primarily under the control of third parties. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard stated that it meanwhile controlled the necessary data itself and had provided KPMG with more than 200 million data sets relating to December 2019 for a forensic audit. Wirecard represented that this audit had not revealed any deviations between the reported revenues and account balances. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard stated that KPMG had identified documentation and organizational weaknesses during the audit period, and that these weaknesses had already been identified by Wirecard. Wirecard stated that it had been remedying those weaknesses since 2019 by establishing a Global Compliance Organization and with the support of external consultants. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard stated that the release of the annual accounts and the annual press conference would not take place on 30 April 2020. Wirecard stated that it would coordinate with auditor E&Y as soon as possible concerning when the audit measures could be completed, taking into account the restrictions related to COVID-19 and completion of the KPMG report. [SRC-001][1]

The announcement identified the contact as Iris Stöckl, Vice President Corporate Communications/Investor Relations, and included the telephone number, email address, and Wirecard website. [SRC-001][1]

The announcement identified Wirecard AG as a company located at Einsteinring 35, 85609 Aschheim near Munich, Germany. It listed:
- ISIN: DE0007472060;
- Reuters identifier: WDI.GDE;
- Bloomberg identifier: WDI GY;
- EQS News ID: 1031139.

It stated that Wirecard was listed on the Regulated Market in Frankfurt, Prime Standard, and on the Regulated Unofficial Markets in Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Munich, Stuttgart, and Tradegate. It also stated that Wirecard was included in the DAX, TecDAX, Prime All Share, and Technology All Share indices. [SRC-001][1]

### 1.2 Limits on what the Wirecard statement establishes

The Wirecard announcement establishes what Wirecard publicly asserted on 28 April 2020. It does not, on the supplied record, independently establish that:
- balance-sheet forgery did not occur;
- the reported revenues were accurate;
- the reported account balances existed;
- the KPMG report found no misconduct;
- the trust-account funds existed or were accessible;
- the audit evidence was complete;
- auditor E&Y ultimately completed the audit successfully; or
- any particular person, including Jan Marsalek, participated in or caused any alleged misconduct.

The announcement itself acknowledged that “not all data could be obtained” that KPMG would have required to prove revenues for 2016–2018 because the relevant data were primarily controlled by third parties. [SRC-001][1]

The supplied source record does not include the KPMG report itself, the later auditor findings, the 18 June 2020 events concerning the alleged €1.9 billion, or any source establishing what happened to Jan Marsalek.

---

## 2. Audit findings, qualifications, delays, limitations, and uncertainty

### 2.1 KPMG special investigation as described by Wirecard

According to Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 disclosure, KPMG had delivered a special audit report to Wirecard. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard characterized the report as not identifying incriminating evidence for the public allegations of balance-sheet forgery. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard stated that no significant findings had been made in four areas that would require adjustments to the 2016–2018 annual accounts:
1. Third Party Acquiring business;
2. Merchant Cash Advance/Digital Lending;
3. business activities in India; and
4. business activities in Singapore. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard stated that the documents and audit measures available during the audits of the 2016–2018 annual accounts were sufficient to prove Third Party Acquiring revenues. [SRC-001][1]

However, Wirecard also stated that the enhanced forensic requirements applied by KPMG could not be fully satisfied because not all required data could be obtained. The stated reason was that the necessary data were primarily in the control of third parties. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard stated that more than 200 million December 2019 data sets had been supplied to KPMG for forensic audit after Wirecard came to control the necessary data itself. Wirecard represented that the forensic audit had found no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard stated that KPMG identified documentation and organizational weaknesses, which Wirecard said it had already identified. Wirecard stated that it was addressing them through a Global Compliance Organization and external consultants. [SRC-001][1]

### 2.2 Delay in publication of annual accounts and annual press conference

Wirecard stated that the release of its annual accounts and the annual press conference would not occur on 30 April 2020. [SRC-001][1]

Wirecard stated that it would coordinate with E&Y concerning completion of the audit measures, while taking into account:
- COVID-19-related restrictions; and
- completion of the KPMG report. [SRC-001][1]

The supplied source does not establish the eventual date of completion of those measures, the date of publication of annual accounts, or the final position of E&Y.

### 2.3 Audit uncertainty and evidentiary limitations

The record contains a material qualification in Wirecard’s own description: the ordinary audit procedures and available documents were described as sufficient to prove revenues, but KPMG’s increased forensic requirements could not be fully met because not all required data were available. [SRC-001][1]

Accordingly, the following propositions must remain distinct:
- **Wirecard’s representation:** available documents and audit measures were sufficient for proof of Third Party Acquiring revenues for the 2016–2018 audits. [SRC-001][1]
- **Wirecard’s acknowledged limitation:** KPMG could not obtain all data required under its increased forensic requirements because the data were primarily controlled by third parties. [SRC-001][1]
- **Wirecard’s representation about additional data:** more than 200 million December 2019 data sets were provided to KPMG, and that forensic audit found no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. [SRC-001][1]
- **Unresolved point in the supplied record:** the record does not include the underlying KPMG work papers, the complete KPMG report, or an independent source confirming the completeness or reliability of the data.

---

## 3. Missing or inaccessible cash, trust-account evidence, and factual discrepancies

The supplied tool results do **not** provide a source record concerning:
- €1.9 billion allegedly held in trust accounts;
- missing or inaccessible Wirecard cash;
- trustee-bank confirmations;
- the existence or nonexistence of the relevant trust accounts;
- discrepancies between Wirecard’s representations and bank evidence;
- the final audit position of E&Y;
- the role of Wirecard executives in any missing-cash allegations; or
- any factual findings concerning the destination of the allegedly missing funds.

The only cash- or account-related information in the supplied record is Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 representation that a forensic audit of more than 200 million December 2019 data sets had revealed “no deviations between the reported revenues and account balances.” [SRC-001][1]

That representation is not the same as evidence that particular cash funds existed in particular trust accounts. The supplied source does not establish the identity of any trustee, bank, account, signatory, beneficiary, or transaction.

The supplied record therefore contains a significant evidentiary gap concerning the missing-cash and trust-account dimension.

---

## 4. Documented failures, omissions, investigations, criticisms, and allegations concerning supervisory and regulatory bodies

### 4.1 Scope and character of the European Parliament-commissioned study

The second source is a study titled **“What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?”** It was prepared by the Economic Governance Support Unit of the European Parliament’s Directorate-General for Internal Policies, requested by the European Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs. The study is identified as **PE 651.385**, with a November 2020 English edition. [SRC-002][2]

The authors identified in the source are:
- Katja Langenbucher, Goethe University Frankfurt and Sciences Po Paris;
- Christian Leuz, University of Chicago Booth School of Business and NBER;
- Jan Pieter Krahnen, Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE and Goethe University; and
- Loriana Pelizzon, Leibniz Institute for Financial Research SAFE, Goethe University and Ca’ Foscari University of Venice. [SRC-002][2]

The document states that its opinions are the sole responsibility of the authors and do not necessarily represent the official position of the European Parliament. [SRC-002][2]

The document also states that Katja Langenbucher is a member of BaFin’s Supervisory Board, but that the opinions expressed in the paper are entirely her own and do not reflect a position taken by BaFin. [SRC-002][2]

The study’s abstract states that it discusses the policy implications of the Wirecard scandal. It states that “all lines of defense against corporate fraud,” including internal control systems, external audits, oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing, and the market supervisor, contributed to the scandal and are in need of reform. [SRC-002][2]

The study states that its purpose was to make eight suggestions for the market and institutional oversight architecture in Germany and Europe to ensure market integrity and investor protection in the future. [SRC-002][2]

### 4.2 Assessments concerning the five lines of defense

The study’s executive summary states:

> “In our view, all five lines of defence against corporate fraud and deception have failed in one way or another: the company’s internal control system, its supervisory board, its external audit, the oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing and, last but not least, the market supervisor BaFin.” [SRC-002][2]

The study states that the slow unraveling of Wirecard was surprising because there were a number of signals suggesting fraudulent behavior years before its eventual revelation. [SRC-002][2]

The authors identify what they describe as a root cause: a flawed market and institutional oversight architecture implicating all five lines of defense. They state that, in its current form, the architecture is not sufficiently fit to preserve market integrity and investor protection. [SRC-002][2]

The study describes the Wirecard scandal in Germany as potentially a pivotal event for Europe’s capital market and as a possible trigger for regulatory reform of financial-market oversight that could improve the competitiveness of European capital markets. [SRC-002][2]

These statements are the authors’ assessments and policy conclusions. They are not, on the supplied record, judicial findings or admissions by BaFin, Wirecard, E&Y, KPMG, FREP, APAS, or any other body. [SRC-002][2]

### 4.3 Recommendations concerning information flows and oversight

The study’s policy conclusions state that capital-market integrity should be supported by strengthening accountability. [SRC-002][2]

The authors propose improving the flow of information to markets and supervisors and respecting whistleblowing and short selling as important information sources. [SRC-002][2]

The study states that the accountability of external auditors should be strengthened so that auditors have stronger incentives to detect accounting manipulations and fraud. It connects this recommendation to improving the information value of audits for capital markets and, ultimately, the accuracy and credibility of firms’ financial reporting. [SRC-002][2]

To strengthen internal controls, the study recommends that listed firms be legally required to maintain an appropriate and effective internal control system. It recommends that the head of internal control report to the supervisory board rather than the management board. It also states that internal-control audits should be considered. [SRC-002][2]

### 4.4 Assessments and recommendations concerning BaFin and FREP

The study states that BaFin needs “considerably stronger supervisory and enforcement powers” to fulfill its overarching mandate concerning market integrity and investor protection. [SRC-002][2]

It recommends giving BaFin broad enforcement powers, including forensic and investigative tools. [SRC-002][2]

The study also states that these changes would entail relegating self-regulatory enforcement bodies such as FREP in Germany to a purely ancillary, optional function. [SRC-002][2]

The supplied excerpt identifies the report’s contents as including:
- markets, oversight, and the Wirecard case;
- weaknesses of market and institutional oversight;
- blocked information flows;
- weaknesses in external audits, internal oversight, and market forces;
- impaired enforcement of financial-information disclosure;
- the overarching mandate and accountability of the market supervisor;
- conclusions;
- an appendix concerning facts and timeline; and
- an appendix concerning supervisory architectures across Europe. [SRC-002][2]

The supplied record does not include the full text of those sections. It therefore does not establish specific factual findings about individual acts or omissions by BaFin, FREP, APAS, E&Y, KPMG, Wirecard’s supervisory board, or other named bodies beyond the study’s general assessments quoted above.

---

## 5. Jan Marsalek’s disappearance

The supplied source records contain **no information** about Jan Marsalek’s disappearance.

They do not establish:
- the date on which Marsalek disappeared;
- his last verified location;
- his movements;
- whether he left Germany voluntarily or involuntarily;
- whether he used assistance;
- the identity or role of any participant;
- whether any person aided, directed, financed, or concealed his departure;
- whether his disappearance was connected to Wirecard’s financial affairs;
- whether he was accused, charged, or convicted of any offense;
- his current whereabouts; or
- the circumstances, causation, or participants involved in his disappearance.

No verified fact about Marsalek’s disappearance, and no clearly stated official unknown, appears in the supplied tool excerpts. Any further assertion would go beyond the source record.

---

## 6. Contradictions and gaps in the supplied record

### 6.1 Wirecard’s representations versus the existence of underlying evidence

Wirecard represented on 28 April 2020 that:
- no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified;
- no significant findings required adjustments to the 2016–2018 annual accounts;
- available documents and audit measures were sufficient to prove Third Party Acquiring revenues;
- more than 200 million December 2019 data sets had been provided to KPMG; and
- the forensic audit found no deviations between reported revenues and account balances. [SRC-001][1]

The same announcement stated that KPMG could not obtain all data required under its increased forensic requirements because the relevant data were primarily under the control of third parties. [SRC-001][1]

This is not necessarily a direct contradiction, but it creates an evidentiary limitation: the source simultaneously reports Wirecard’s positive representations and Wirecard’s acknowledgment that the enhanced forensic evidence set was incomplete.

### 6.2 Later cash and trust-account issues are not covered

The supplied records do not contain the later evidence needed to compare Wirecard’s April 2020 representations with:
- the alleged absence or inaccessibility of cash;
- trustee-account confirmations;
- bank records;
- E&Y’s final audit position; or
- subsequent investigative or judicial findings.

Therefore, the supplied record cannot establish whether those later matters contradicted the April 2020 representations.

### 6.3 Supervisory-failure assessment versus primary factual findings

The European Parliament-commissioned study assesses that all five lines of defense failed in one way or another and that BaFin required stronger powers. [SRC-002][2]

The study expressly states that its opinions are those of its authors and do not necessarily represent the official position of the European Parliament. [SRC-002][2]

The source record does not include primary investigative findings, official admissions, court determinations, or agency decisions that independently establish each alleged failure. The study’s statements must therefore be identified as assessments and policy conclusions rather than treated as independently verified adjudicated facts.

### 6.4 Marsalek disappearance gap

No supplied source addresses Marsalek’s disappearance. The record therefore cannot support any conclusion about its timing, circumstances, participants, causation, or whereabouts.
